title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 27
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Light Nobody Can Be Charged For
passages.text:
A. The lighthouse occupies an odd position in economic argument because it was for a long time the standard example of something markets cannot supply. A light visible from the sea cannot be withheld from a ship that has not paid for it, and cannot be used up by being used, so no operator can collect from the vessels benefiting. The conclusion drawn was that lighthouses must be provided by the state or not at all.

B. The historical record complicates that conclusion without overturning it. Many lights were in fact built and operated privately, under arrangements where the operator was granted the right to collect a charge from ships at the ports they served. Collection happened at the harbour, where a vessel could be identified and could not avoid payment, rather than at sea where it could not — a solution that worked by finding a chokepoint rather than by disproving the underlying problem.

C. What the lights had to do was harder than it appears. A single steady flame tells a navigator that land is near and nothing about which land, which is precisely the information needed. The development of distinct flash patterns, each unique within a stretch of coast, turned a warning into an identification, and required clockwork, lenses and a standard of manufacture that took a long time to achieve reliably.

D. Optics did more for range than fire ever could. Increasing the light source's power raised output slowly and fuel consumption quickly; capturing light that would otherwise scatter and directing it towards the horizon raised effective range dramatically for the same fuel. The stepped lens developed for the purpose is one of the clearest cases of an optical device outperforming brute increases in power, and it remained in use long after the light behind it changed.

E. The keepers' role has been almost entirely mythologised in one direction and neglected in another. The isolation and heroism are real and much described; the routine — cleaning, winding, logging weather, maintaining machinery in salt air — was the actual work, and it was the reliability of that routine rather than any dramatic episode that kept ships off rocks. Automation removed the keepers and the failure rate did not rise.

F. Satellite positioning has made the lights redundant in principle and they have not been removed, for reasons worth examining. Electronic systems fail, are jammed or spoofed, and depend on equipment that a small vessel may not carry or maintain; a light requires nothing of the observer. Retaining a system that duplicates a better one is usually waste and is occasionally the difference between a redundant system and a single point of failure.

passages.title: The Passengers
passages.text:
The human body carries an enormous population of bacteria, concentrated in the large intestine, in numbers comparable to the body's own cells. That this population exists has been known for a long time. What has changed recently is the ability to identify its members without growing them in a laboratory, since most of them cannot be grown, and the resulting flood of data has produced both genuine discoveries and a quantity of overstatement that the field is still working through.

The established findings are substantial. These bacteria digest material human enzymes cannot, producing compounds the body uses; they occupy space and resources that would otherwise be available to organisms that cause disease; and they are necessary for the normal development of the immune system, as animals raised without them develop abnormally in ways that can be corrected by introducing bacteria. None of this is in dispute.

The difficulty lies in the step from association to cause, and it is where most reporting goes wrong. Differences in bacterial populations have been found between people with and without a long list of conditions, and the finding is real in each case. Whether the difference caused the condition, resulted from it, or followed from something producing both — diet being the obvious candidate, since it changes bacterial populations within days — is a separate question that association studies cannot settle.

Transfer experiments in animals are the strongest evidence available and are weaker than they are usually reported to be. Transferring bacteria from an affected animal to an unaffected one sometimes transfers the characteristic, which is a genuine causal demonstration in that system. Whether it generalises to humans, whose bacterial populations differ substantially and whose conditions are less cleanly defined, is exactly the question at issue, and mice are not a settled answer to it.

The clinical position is narrower than the coverage suggests. One transfer procedure is established treatment for a specific recurrent infection, with a success rate high enough that the evidence is not seriously contested. For everything else — mood, weight, immune conditions, general wellbeing — the evidence supports investigation rather than treatment, and the commercial products sold on the strength of it typically contain organisms that do not establish themselves and are gone within days of stopping.

The honest summary is that this is a real and important system, at an early stage of being understood, sold as though it were at a late one. That combination has a familiar shape, and the appropriate response to it is neither dismissal nor enthusiasm but attention to which specific claim is being made and what supports it.

passages.title: Promises Against the Future
passages.text:
A pension is a claim on output that has not yet been produced. Whatever form the arrangement takes — a government promise, an employer's obligation, a fund of shares and bonds — what a retired person ultimately consumes is goods and services made by people working at that time. This is the fact that most pension argument obscures, and holding onto it dissolves several apparent controversies.

The distinction usually drawn is between funded schemes, which accumulate assets, and pay-as-you-go schemes, in which current contributions pay current pensions. The distinction is real for the individual and considerably less real for the economy. A pensioner with a large fund sells assets to working people in order to consume; a pensioner with a state entitlement receives transfers from working people. In both cases the working population hands over part of current output, and in both cases the terms depend on how much output there is and how many people are claiming a share.

Demographic change therefore bites regardless of scheme design. A population with proportionally fewer workers and more retirees faces the same arithmetic whether its pensions are funded or not: if many people are selling assets to fewer buyers, asset prices adjust, and the fund buys less than expected. Funding changes who holds the risk and how visible it is, and does not remove the underlying constraint.

Three responses exist and all are unpopular in different constituencies. Contributions can rise, benefits can fall, or the retirement age can rise; increases in productivity or in the number of workers help, and neither is straightforwardly available as policy. Countries that have adjusted early and gradually have done so through some combination of the three, and those that have delayed have generally made larger and more abrupt versions of the same adjustments later.

Retirement ages carry a difficulty that aggregate life expectancy conceals. Life expectancy has risen substantially and unevenly, and the difference between occupational groups is large enough that a uniform increase asks considerably more of people in physically demanding work with shorter lives than of professionals with longer ones. Uniform rules applied to a non-uniform population produce a regressive outcome that the aggregate statistic hides entirely.

The framing of this as intergenerational conflict is the part that deserves most resistance. Every worker paying into a scheme is a future claimant, and every retiree drawing from one contributed under the rules that then applied. What is actually being decided is how the cost of a demographic change nobody chose is divided, and presenting it as a contest between age groups obscures both that the change was foreseeable decades ago and that the choice remains available to make the adjustment gradually.
